Turf built for Narcoossee's wells, septic tanks and big yards

Installed artificial grass runs $8–$18 per square foot in Narcoossee as of September 2026, the same Central Florida range whether the lot is a quarter acre in Lake Ajay Village or several acres of former grove land off Narcoossee Road. Most of the ground here maps to the Narcoossee, Smyrna or Myakka soil series, all of it slow to drain once the summer water table climbs.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Grading for a water table that climbs every summer

Two named soil series cover most of the area: the Narcoossee series itself, established here in 1976 and mapped on the low sandy knolls threaded through the flatwoods, and Smyrna sand in the lower ground between them, also first classified in Osceola County that same year (the Narcoossee series description; the Smyrna series description). Both hold a water table that climbs to within two or three feet of the surface for months at a stretch, and Smyrna's lower pockets sit wetter still.

That's shallow enough that a thin four-inch rock layer only just clears the wet season's high point, which is why crews working this ground lean toward the deeper end of what the state allows rather than splitting the difference, especially at a yard's low corner, where Myakka sand, the true depression soil in the mix, tends to take over (the Myakka series description).

Why infill grain size matters for staying on the property

The state's rule that infill must not wash off a lawn puts some weight on grain size, not just infill type, when choosing a product for a Narcoossee yard with any real slope to it. A finer, lighter sand can lift and travel toward a low corner during a hard rain faster than a coarser grade of the same silica sand would, even though both meet the natural-material requirement. On a lawn graded toward a swale or a shared boundary, choosing a slightly heavier grain, and keeping the grade itself gentle, does more to keep infill in place than switching infill types altogether.

Say you have a 2.5-acre lot off Narcoossee Road

Say a 2.5-acre property off Narcoossee Road carries a 1980s home, a detached barn and a septic tank whose lid nobody's seen in a decade. The owner wants a defined 1,400 sq ft yard between the back porch and an existing wood fence, leaving the rest as mowed field. At the published $8–$18 per square foot range, that prices between roughly $11,200 and $25,200, with most bids on ground like this landing near $14,000 to $22,400.

Getting there means locating the septic lid first, building the base to the fuller four-inch depth for the site's Myakka-adjacent low corner, and using the existing fence line as the turf's edge anchor instead of a fresh paver border. The barn and the rest of the field stay exactly as they are.

A well and a septic tank change the install, not the price

A house on a private well was never tied to an in-ground zone the way a Toho-fed subdivision lot is, so there's no sprinkler head to cap before turf goes down on most of Narcoossee's larger parcels. What doesn't change is the septic side of the state's rule: the tank's pump-out lid has to stay reachable once the lawn is finished, and on an older acreage lot that lid was often never marked after the original install, buried since under decades of mowing.

We ask for a pump-out receipt or a call to whoever last serviced the tank before laying out where turf can go, and build the base up to the lid's edge rather than over it. A newer, HOA-governed lot in a community such as Lake Ajay Village skips this step but adds the irrigation-capping one instead.

Why a lawn can't cross a swale or hug a pond

Two setbacks apply to any Narcoossee lawn near water: turf has to stay at least ten feet from a natural or man-made waterbody unless a seawall or bulkhead already separates the two, and it can never go inside a drainage swale, ditch, or a stormwater pond's littoral zone, no matter how flat and convenient that strip of ground looks. Both rules exist because turf and the base under it change how water moves across a lot, and a swale or pond edge is specifically where the state doesn't want that changed. A yard backing onto a retention pond usually has more usable space than these setbacks first suggest, just not right up to the water's edge.

Why the subgrade slopes away from the house

Grade comes before rock on a Narcoossee lawn: the bare soil gets shaped to fall one to two percent moving away from the foundation, following the direction water was already heading before construction started, whether that's toward a rear fence line, a side yard low point, or a street-facing curb. That fall gets rechecked with a level once the first lift of rock is compacted, since two to four inches of stone can flatten a subtle slope if nobody's watching for it. A lawn shaped this way sends a downpour toward the yard's natural low spot instead of pooling against the house, which is the entire point of doing this step in Narcoossee before turf ever gets involved.

Why an acreage lot usually turfs a yard, not a property

A multi-acre parcel off Narcoossee Road isn't priced or built as though the whole property needs to be lawn. Most owners define a yard close to the house, porch to fence line or porch to the first line of old grove trees, and leave the rest as pasture, mowed field or native scrub. That decision changes the math more than the soil does: a defined yard costs the same per square foot whether the surrounding parcel runs a fifth of an acre or five, and the crew still measures, grades and bases only the section that gets turfed.

Open acreage does add one detail a tighter Buenaventura Lakes lot skips: without a next-door fence line a few feet away, edge anchoring along an open pasture boundary has to hold against wind with nothing nearby to break it.

Scheduling a lawn install around a Narcoossee rainy season

Rainy season in Central Florida runs June through September, with afternoon storms arriving on a near-daily schedule by midsummer, and that pattern shapes when a Narcoossee lawn conversion gets scheduled more than most homeowners expect. Base compaction needs the ground reasonably dry to pack correctly, so a crew working through a wet stretch may pause a job partway through rather than compact rock into standing water. Dry-season installs, roughly October through May, tend to move start to finish without a weather-driven gap, which is part of why booking calendars fill up fastest in the cooler months even though the work itself is identical either time of year.

Rinsing a lawn instead of watering it

A synthetic lawn never gets watered through an in-ground system, since the state's rule bars using irrigation heads on turf and any that used to serve the area get capped at installation. A hose rinse takes over that job instead, settling infill, clearing pollen, and cooling the surface 30 to 50 degrees on a hot Narcoossee afternoon within minutes of turning the water on. Rinsing more often in peak summer than in a mild spring is normal, and there's no schedule to keep beyond doing it when the lawn looks dusty, smells faintly of pollen, or simply feels too hot to walk across barefoot.

Questions people ask

Do I need a permit to convert a Narcoossee lawn to turf?

Osceola County’s Building Department reviews it, since Narcoossee has no city hall of its own. Its Land Development Code doesn't name synthetic turf, so the application goes through ordinary landscape and drainage review plus the state's rule rather than a local turf-specific standard.

Does a five-acre lot cost more to turf than a quarter-acre one?

Not if the finished yard is the same size. Price follows the square footage that actually gets turfed, not the acreage around it, so a 1,200 sq ft yard prices the same whether it sits on a fifth of an acre in Lake Ajay Village or in the middle of five acres of former grove land.
